summary: Allison Miller, a Virginia communications director, lost her left leg above the knee a decade ago after flu at age 33 led to bilateral bacterial pneumonia, sepsis, septic shock and life support. She urges everyone to get a yearly flu vaccine and to seek medical care early when symptoms are severe. CSL Seqirus's Dr. Gregg Sylvester says vaccination reduces severe complications and that mid-October is a good time to get vaccinated.
one_line: A Virginia woman who lost her leg after flu-related pneumonia and septic shock urges everyone to get vaccinated and seek care early.
key_facts: Allison Miller, a Virginia-based communications director, was 33 and healthy when flu complications led to the loss of her left leg; this year marks a decade since.
Miller's influenza caused bilateral bacterial pneumonia, which affects both lungs and is more severe than viral pneumonia, then sepsis and septic shock.
Miller was put on life support in the ICU; after five days she had a rare complication of lost blood circulation that required amputation.
Doctors amputated Miller's left leg above the knee while she was in a medically induced coma, and she woke after about three weeks.
Miller spent two more months in the hospital and weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, and now walks with a prosthesis.
Miller still has permanent lung damage, below-average heart function, and a terminal lung condition needing regular treatment.
Miller did not get a flu vaccine that year because she had 'missed the memo that flu vaccines were for everyone.'
Miller says her illness went from onset to the ICU within 24 to 48 hours.

Dr. Gregg Sylvester of CSL Seqirus says flu inflames the respiratory tract and can let secondary bacteria enter, and that vaccination makes severe complications markedly less common and symptoms milder.
Sylvester called mid-October the 'perfect time' to get a flu vaccine as U.S. cases begin to rise, though 'it's never too late.'
In the 2021-2022 flu season, the CDC estimated nine million illnesses, four million medical visits, 10,000 hospitalizations and 5,000 deaths.
The CDC recommends that everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine every season, with rare exceptions.
